questions.question: 1(a)
questions.summary: Identify two reasons why using a handheld gimbal with mobile phones has recently increased in popularity.
questions.prompt:
Fig. 1.1 shows a mobile phone in a handheld gimbal, a device that uses a set of motors and sensors to keep the phone steady, so that smooth video shots can be recorded.

Identify two reasons why using a handheld gimbal with mobile phones has recently increased in popularity. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
One mark for identifying each of two reasons why using a handheld gimbal with mobile phones has recently increased in popularity (max 2 marks):
• Social media increasingly encourages people to post personal videos (1)
• The cost of gimbals is steadily reducing (1)
• The improving technology is making gimbals lighter and more portable (1)
• Users like the quality of the videos that can be shot (1)
• Any other valid suggestion.

questions.question: 1(b)
questions.summary: Identify three issues a design engineering company would investigate before investing in developing a new handheld gimbal.
questions.prompt:
A design engineering company is considering whether to invest in developing a new handheld gimbal for use with mobile phones.

Identify three issues the company would need to investigate before deciding whether to proceed. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
One mark for identifying each of three issues the company would need to investigate before deciding whether to proceed (max 3 marks):
• Analysis of the environment in which the product may be used (1)
• User requirements / stakeholder needs (1)
• Types and sizes of phones / cameras (1)
• Economic / market considerations (1)
• Existing product / SWOT analysis (1)
• Ways of raising capital (1)
• Technology available – motors / batteries etc. (1)
• Any other valid suggestion.

questions.question: 1(c)(i)
questions.summary: Discuss possible limitations when using the 3-axis handheld gimbal control system.
questions.prompt:
Fig. 1.2a shows an annotated diagram of the handheld gimbal control system (camera, handle, yaw motor, roll motor, pitch motor). Three motors are used to stabilise the camera in the three axes of pitch, roll and yaw as shown in Fig. 1.2b.

Sensors are located at specific points around the handheld gimbal. When the sensors detect movement of the camera in each of the three axes, the motors counteract that motion almost instantly. The system is controlled by a microcontroller.

The handheld gimbal can remove most, but not all, of the unwanted motion caused by the movements of the user’s hand.

Discuss possible limitations when using the handheld gimbal control system. [6]
questions.markscheme_text:
Level 3 (5–6 marks): Clear understanding of the handheld gimbal control system. Thorough discussion explaining a number of limitations from multiple perspectives.
Level 2 (3–4 marks): Reasonable understanding. Sound discussion explaining limitations resulting from system use.
Level 1 (1–2 marks): Basic descriptive knowledge with little appreciation of limitations.

Indicative content:
• Control system may not be fast enough to respond to rapid hand movements, especially in filming faster motion.
• High-frequency vibration may be too fast for the system to respond to.
• Processing speed of microcontroller may be too slow to react to sudden movements, resulting in missed movements and erratic responses.
• Inertia of the mechanical system will slow down response time.
• Limited motor torque will slow response time and limit allowable size/weight of camera unit.
• Motors may not rotate full 360° (mechanical end stops limit travel).
• Non-rotational movements (linear translation along X, Y, or Z axis) will not be cancelled out.
• Total weight of phone mount, motors, and batteries causes fatigue for user.
• Any other valid suggestion.

questions.question: 1(c)(ii)
questions.summary: Calculate the angle through which the gimbal tilted based on potentiometer voltage change.
questions.prompt:
Fig. 1.3 shows a prototype system for sensing the angle of tilt of an object. It consists of a pendulum, freely pivoted on a potentiometer (a variable resistor). Data for the potentiometer is given below:
• Full rotation angle: 300°
• Track resistance: 10 kΩ

The potentiometer is connected in the circuit shown in Fig. 1.4 (powered by 5 V DC across the 10 kΩ track).
When the gimbal is held horizontal to the ground, the potentiometer output voltage (V_out) is 2.50 V.
When the gimbal is tilted the V_out rises to 2.70 V.

Calculate the angle through which the gimbal has tilted. Show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 3 marks as follows:
• Increase in V_out: 2.70 V – 2.50 V = 0.20 V (1 mark)
• Sensitivity / Volt per degree: 5 V / 300° = 0.0167 V/degree (to 3 s.f.) (1 mark)
• Angle turned = 0.20 V / (5 / 300) = 12° (Allow 11.9° to 12.1°) (1 mark)
(If correct answer 12° is given without working out shown, award full marks. ECF applies.)

questions.question: 1(c)(iii)
questions.summary: Explain one reason why the sensor specification is suitable for use on the handheld gimbal.
questions.prompt:
Data for the actual sensor used on the handheld gimbal is given below:
• Power supply: 1.8 to 3.6 V
• Power consumption: < 1 mW
• Sensitivity: 0.005g

Explain one reason why this sensor is suitable for use on the handheld gimbal. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
One mark for analysing the data in the table to identify a reason; one mark for explaining why it is suitable on the gimbal (2 marks):
• Wide power supply range (1.8–3.6 V) (1): will suit a variety of single-cell or multi-cell battery packs without needing complex voltage regulation (1).
• Low power consumption (< 1 mW) (1): ensures the battery will last a long time during extended handheld filming sessions (1).
• High sensitivity (0.005g) (1): enables minute hand tremors and slight vibrations to be detected quickly and corrected (1).

questions.question: 1(d)(i)
questions.summary: Explain one reason why modern materials such as rare earth magnets are used in electric motors.
questions.prompt:
Electric motors as used in the handheld gimbal often make use of modern materials such as rare earth magnets.

Explain one reason why modern materials are used in electric motors. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Up to 2 marks for explaining why modern materials are used in electric motors:
• Modern materials such as rare earth magnets have a very strong magnetic field / high flux density (1). This enables the motor to produce a high torque / be very compact and lightweight / be very powerful for its size (1).
• High-performance alloys enable the rotor to be lightweight (1), allowing the rotor to spin at higher speeds and respond rapidly with low rotational inertia (1).
(Do not accept smart material-based answers.)

questions.question: 1(d)(ii)
questions.summary: State one type of motor suitable for use in the handheld gimbal and explain why it would be used.
questions.prompt: State one type of motor that would be suitable for use in the handheld gimbal and explain why it would be used. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
One mark for identifying a suitable motor; one mark for explaining why it would be suitable (2 marks):
• Brushless DC motor (BLDC) (1): High torque-to-weight ratio, high efficiency, can hold fine angular positions smoothly without brush friction, and very quiet in operation (1).
• Servo motor (1): Rotates to a given commanded angular position then holds, provides fast response and high closed-loop torque (1).
• Stepper motor (1): Rotates through precise discrete step angles per pulse, provides high holding torque without slip (1).

questions.question: 1(d)(iii)
questions.summary: Explain using sketches and/or notes how the motor identified in part (ii) could be controlled.
questions.prompt:
Explain, using sketches and/or notes, how the motor you identified in part (ii) could be controlled.

You should:
• identify the signals required for the motor to operate correctly;
• explain how these signals affect the direction, speed and position of the motor. [4]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 4 marks as follows:
• Signals required (1 mark): Identifies connection wires and control signal (e.g. Servo: 3 wires — Red +V, Black 0V, White PWM pulse signal; Brushless/Stepper: multi-phase driver connections).
• Direction of motor (1 mark): Explains how signals affect direction (e.g. Servo: pulse width compared to center 1.5ms pulse determines clockwise/counter-clockwise travel; Brushless/Stepper: sequence of phase excitation determines forward or reverse direction).
• Speed of motor (1 mark): Explains how signals affect speed (e.g. Servo: rate of pulse width change / gearing; Brushless/Stepper: pulse frequency / commutation switching rate controls rotational velocity).
• Position of motor (1 mark): Explains how signals affect position (e.g. Servo: duty cycle pulse width 1.0ms–2.0ms maps proportionally to 0°–180° angular position; Stepper: total number of step pulses determines final angular displacement).

questions.question: 2(a)
questions.summary: Draw on a 10mm grid an accurate 2D elevation of an isometric part with hidden detail lines.
questions.prompt:
Fig. 2.1 shows a 3-dimensional isometric projection of a part (overall dimensions 60 mm × 60 mm × 40 mm with 20 mm uprights, a 10 mm thick baseplate, and a Ø20 mm hole centred in the baseplate).

Draw, on a 10 mm grid, an accurate 2-dimensional elevation of the part from direction A. Indicate any hidden lines. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 3 marks as follows:
• One mark for analysing Fig. 2.1 to correctly outline the U-shape (1 mark).
• One mark for correct dimensions on grid paper (60 mm wide, 40 mm high uprights, 20 mm wide upright columns, 10 mm high baseplate) (1 mark).
• One mark for correct hidden detail lines representing the Ø20 mm hole and baseplate recess (dashed lines) (1 mark).

questions.question: 2(b)
questions.summary: Calculate the horizontal spread length S of a camera tripod leg using trigonometry.
questions.prompt:
Fig. 2.2a shows one leg of a camera tripod. Fig. 2.2b shows the right-angled triangle formed by one leg of the tripod (hypotenuse leg length = 385 mm, apex angle = 27°, base side = S).

Using the information from Fig. 2.2b, calculate the length of S correct to the nearest mm. Show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 3 marks as follows:
• Apply trigonometry formula: sin(27°) = S / 385 (1 mark)
• Manipulate formula: S = 385 × sin(27°) = 174.79 mm (1 mark)
• Round answer to nearest mm: S = 175 mm (1 mark)
(Full marks if correct answer 175 mm is given without working. Working must be shown for partial credit.)

questions.question: 2(c)(i)
questions.summary: Calculate the tensile force F exerted on a bicycle brake cable from a 25 N lever force.
questions.prompt:
Fig. 2.3 shows a bicycle brake lever. The rider exerts a 25 N force at an 85 mm lever distance from the fulcrum. The brake cable is attached at 40 mm from the fulcrum.

Using the information from Fig. 2.3, calculate the tensile force F exerted on the cable when the rider exerts a 25 N force at the end of the brake lever. Show your working. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 2 marks as follows:
• Lever arm ratio / Principle of Moments: 85 mm / 40 mm = 2.125 (or 25 × 85 = F × 40) (1 mark)
• Tensile force F = 25 N × 2.125 = 53.125 N (or 53.1 N) (1 mark)
(Full marks if correct answer is given without working out. ECF applies.)

questions.question: 2(c)(ii)
questions.summary: Calculate the cross-sectional area of a 1.6 mm diameter stainless steel wire in m².
questions.prompt:
The cable is made from stainless steel. It has an unstretched length of 1500 mm and a diameter of 1.6 mm.

Calculate the cross sectional area of the wire in m² to 3 significant figures. Show your working.
Area of a circle = πr² [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 3 marks as follows:
• Radius r = 1.6 mm / 2 = 0.8 mm (1 mark)
• Convert mm into m: 0.8 mm = 0.0008 m = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ m (1 mark)
• Area A = π × (0.0008)² = 2.01 × 10⁻⁶ m² (to 3 s.f.) (1 mark)
(Full marks if correct answer is given without working out. ECF applies.)

questions.question: 2(c)(iii)
questions.summary: Calculate tensile stress in the wire in Pa (N/m²) under a tensile force of 300 N.
questions.prompt: Calculate the stress in the wire in Pa (N·m⁻²) when a tensile force of 300 N is applied to the end of the cable. Show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 3 marks as follows:
• Formula: Stress σ = Force / Cross-sectional Area (1 mark)
• Substitution: Stress = 300 N / 2.01 × 10⁻⁶ m² (1 mark)
• Stress = 1.49 × 10⁸ Pa (N·m⁻²) or 149 MPa (also accept 149,253,731 Pa) (1 mark)
(Full marks if correct answer is given without working out. ECF applies.)

questions.question: 2(c)(iv)
questions.summary: Calculate the extension of the stainless steel cable in mm using Young's modulus.
questions.prompt:
Calculate the extension of the cable in mm to 3 significant figures. Show your working.
Young’s modulus of stainless steel = 180 GPa [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 3 marks as follows:
• Young's Modulus equation: E = Stress / Strain ⇒ 180 × 10⁹ = 149 × 10⁶ / Strain (1 mark)
• Calculate Strain: ε = 149 × 10⁶ / 180 × 10⁹ = 0.000828 (or 8.28 × 10⁻⁴) (1 mark)
• Calculate Extension: ΔL = Strain × Original length = 0.000828 × 1500 mm = 1.24 mm (to 3 s.f.) (1 mark)
(Full marks if correct answer is given without working out. ECF applies.)

questions.question: 2(d)(i)
questions.summary: Calculate the percentage of ladder users with a body mass above 90 kg from a histogram.
questions.prompt:
A ladder manufacturer carried out a survey on the body masses of 30 users. A histogram of the results is shown in Fig. 2.4.

Calculate the percentage of users in the survey who had a body mass above 90 kg. Show your working. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 2 marks as follows:
• Users above 90 kg: 2 (in 90–95 kg bin) + 1 (in 95–100 kg bin) = 3 users (1 mark)
• Percentage: (3 / 30) × 100 = 10% (1 mark)
(Full marks if correct answer 10% is given without working out.)

questions.question: 2(d)(ii)
questions.summary: Show that the 50th percentile body mass of the ladder user sample is less than 84 kg.
questions.prompt:
Anthropometric data for the UK population states that the 50th percentile body mass is 84 kg.

Show that the 50th percentile mass of the sample in Fig. 2.4 is less than 84 kg. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 2 marks as follows:
• Understand that the 50th centile is the median value, which is the 15th / 16th value in the dataset of 30 users (1 mark).
• Cumulative count: 2 + 4 + 5 = 11 (up to 75 kg); + 6 = 17 (up to 80 kg). The median value is in the 75–80 kg class, which is strictly less than 84 kg (1 mark).

questions.question: 3(a)(i)
questions.summary: Describe how a social footprint is created by the manufacture of a product.
questions.prompt:
Designers and manufacturers should consider the social footprint and the ecological footprint of any materials they use.

Describe how a social footprint is created by the manufacture of a product. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Up to 2 marks for describing how a social footprint is created by product manufacture (macro or micro level):
• Mining chemicals or raw materials to make batteries and electronics can scar the landscape and impact local communities (1).
• Building factories to manufacture the product can alter the local environment and community infrastructure (1).
• Creating factory employment stimulates the local economy, skills base, and job market (1).
• Working conditions, worker safety, health standards, and fair wages across global supply chains (1).

questions.question: 3(a)(ii)
questions.summary: Describe the ecological footprint that results when using timber in products.
questions.prompt: Describe the ecological footprint that results when using timber in products. [4]
questions.markscheme_text:
Up to 4 marks for describing the ecological footprint of using timber in products:
• Timber is a natural material requiring extensive forest land to cultivate; while tree growth absorbs carbon dioxide (nearly carbon neutral), fossil energy is required to fell, kiln dry, process, and transport timber to market (1).
• Softwoods (e.g. pine, spruce) grow significantly faster than hardwoods (e.g. oak, beech), producing a smaller ecological footprint in construction and furniture (1).
• Waste sawdust and offcuts created during milling are utilized for biomass fuel or manufactured boards like MDF and chipboard (1).
• Risk of deforestation, habitat destruction, and biodiversity loss if timber is not certified by sustainable forestry bodies (e.g. FSC / PEFC) (1).

questions.question: 3(b)*
questions.summary: Extended response: Discuss how a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) would be carried out on a domestic refrigerator.
questions.prompt:
Discuss how a lifecycle assessment (LCA) would be carried out on a domestic refrigerator.

Make reference to the following stages of the product’s life in your answer:
• manufacture;
• use;
• end of life. [*8]
questions.markscheme_text:
Level 3 (6–8 marks): Clear understanding of LCA. Thorough, well-structured discussion covering manufacture, use, and end-of-life stages for a refrigerator with relevant examples and clear reasoning.
Level 2 (3–5 marks): Reasonable understanding. Sound discussion covering multiple LCA stages for a refrigerator with some structure.
Level 1 (1–2 marks): Basic generic knowledge of LCA with little direct application.

Indicative content:
• Manufacture: Sourcing metals (sheet steel body, copper motor windings, aluminium cooling coils) and polymers (injection moulded ABS liners, polyurethane foam insulation). Toxic refrigerant gasses manufacture. Embodied energy in steel pressing, thermoforming liners, PCB assembly, and factory running energy.
• Use: Continuous 24/7 power draw over 10–15 year lifespan. Energy efficiency rating, improved vacuum/foam thermal insulation to lower compressor duty cycle.
• End of Life: Safe extraction and recycling of refrigerant gas (avoiding greenhouse/ozone depletion). Magnetic sorting and recycling of steel casing and copper coils. Difficulty recycling mixed insulation foam. RoHS directive compliance reducing hazardous substances.
• Transport: Embodied transport carbon moving bulky products from overseas manufacturing hubs.

questions.question: 4(a)
questions.summary: State one reason why the side panels of a washing machine are manufactured with indentations.
questions.prompt:
Fig. 4.1 shows a domestic washing machine.

The side panels of the washing machine shown in Fig. 4.1 are manufactured from a sheet metal with indentations.

State one reason why the side panels have been manufactured in this way. [1]
questions.markscheme_text:
One mark for identifying a reason why the side panels are manufactured in this way (1 mark):
• Adds structural rigidity / stiffness to the thin sheet steel panels without adding extra material or weight (1).
• Dampens vibration and acoustic drum noise during high-speed spinning (1).
• Adds aesthetic styling to the sides of the machine (1).
• Aids moving and lifting the appliance by providing grip indentations (1).

questions.question: 4(b)(i)
questions.summary: Identify three reasons why a belt and pulley drive system is used in a washing machine.
questions.prompt:
Fig. 4.2 shows the belt and pulley drive system between the motor and the washing machine drum (motor pulley diameter 32 mm, drum pulley diameter 384 mm).

Identify three reasons why a belt and pulley drive system would be used in the washing machine. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
One mark for identifying each of three reasons why a belt and pulley drive system is used (max 3 marks):
• Allows for a large reduction in rotational speed from high-speed motor to drum (1).
• Allows a substantial increase in mechanical torque to turn heavy wet laundry (1).
• Allows motor to sit compactly beneath the drum, reducing machine depth (1).
• Allows for a small amount of elastic flexing / shock absorption between motor and drum shafts (1).
• Quiet in operation compared to gear trains or chain drives (1).
(No credit for 'allows slipping' or 'transfers drive from motor to drum'.)

questions.question: 4(b)(ii)
questions.summary: Calculate the rotational speed of the motor when the washing machine drum spins at 1600 rpm.
questions.prompt:
The maximum rotational drum speed is 1600 rpm. The motor pulley has a diameter of 32 mm and the drum pulley has a diameter of 384 mm.

Calculate the rotational speed of the motor when the drum is spinning at maximum speed. Show your working. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 2 marks as follows:
• Pulley ratio (Gear Ratio) = 384 mm / 32 mm = 12 (1 mark)
• Motor rotational speed = 12 × 1600 rpm = 19,200 rpm (1 mark)
(Full marks if correct answer 19,200 rpm is given without working out. ECF applies.)

questions.question: 4(b)(iii)
questions.summary: Describe how a closed loop control system regulates the rotational speed of a washing machine drum.
questions.prompt: Describe how a closed loop control system is used to regulate the rotational speed of the washing machine drum. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Up to 3 marks for describing closed loop drum speed regulation:
• Sensing: The signal from an input transducer (e.g. slotted optical opto-switch, tachogenerator, or Hall effect sensor) measures drum/motor rotational speed (1).
• Feedback comparison: The measured speed signal is fed back to the microcontroller/controller and compared against the target programmed cycle speed (1).
• Actuation error correction: The controller adjusts the electrical drive power (e.g. PWM duty cycle or triac phase angle) to minimize the error difference between feedback speed and setpoint speed (1).

questions.question: 4(c)
questions.summary: Explain two ways in which a graphical display enhances the user interface on a washing machine compared to simple LEDs.
questions.prompt:
User interfaces on early washing machines used simple LED indicators, but many modern washing machines feature graphical displays.

Explain two ways in which a graphical display enhances the user interface on the washing machine. [4]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award up to 4 marks (1 mark for identifying a way, 1 mark for explaining why in context, for each of two ways):
• Rich visual & alphanumeric feedback: Can display more than basic lights, such as exact remaining cycle time, wash temperature, spin speed, and animated tutorials/error diagnostics (1+1).
• Universal international symbols: Can display intuitive icons and multi-lingual text menus, allowing the appliance to be sold globally without redesigning physical control fascia panels (1+1).
• Ergonomics and intuitive navigation: Graphical layouts and icons are clearer to comprehend than cryptic blinking LEDs, reducing human operational errors (1+1).
• Touchscreen / soft keys: Touchscreens reduce physical push buttons, creating a flush, hygienic surface that is easy to wipe clean with a premium luxury aesthetic (1+1).

questions.question: 4(d)*
questions.summary: Extended response: Discuss how destructive and non-destructive testing methods assess a washing machine's suitability for purpose.
questions.prompt: Discuss how the washing machine manufacturer would use destructive and non-destructive testing methods to assess the machine’s suitability for purpose. [*8]
questions.markscheme_text:
Level 3 (6–8 marks): Clear understanding of destructive and non-destructive testing. Thorough discussion explaining how both testing methods judge fitness for purpose across multiple perspectives.
Level 2 (3–5 marks): Reasonable understanding of testing methods. Sound discussion explaining how destructive and/or non-destructive tests assess fitness for purpose.
Level 1 (1–2 marks): Basic generic knowledge of testing with little application.

Indicative content:
• Destructive tests (testing to failure):
- Robotic cyclic door opening/slamming until latch failure.
- Drive belt tensile fatigue pull test until snapping.
- Accelerated life / time-to-failure continuous running tests.
- Overload tests with excess heavy laundry and unbalanced weight distribution.
- Thermal overheat and heater dry-run fire safety tests.
- Electrical overvoltage/spike insulation breakdown tests.
• Non-destructive tests (NDT / QA verification):
- Water pressure leak testing of pumps, valves, and drum seals.
- PAT testing (earth bonding continuity and insulation resistance).
- Failsafe cut-out testing (e.g. door interlock preventing opening during spin).
- Dynamic drum balancing sensor and accelerometer calibration.
- Automated PCB diagnostic test bench and firmware verification.
- Acoustic noise level measurements (dB meter) during 1600 rpm spin.

questions.summary: Critically examine the social, moral and ethical considerations of supplying developing countries with 3D-printed prosthetic limbs.
questions.prompt:
Every year, thousands of people across the world are born without limbs, or lose a limb through accidents. In any society this can be life changing but in the developing world it can have devastating effects across the community.

Charities are looking into the effects of supplying these developing communities with the ability to produce 3D-printed prosthetic limbs to improve the quality of life of those affected.

Critically examine the social, moral and ethical considerations of developing countries being given access to the use of 3D printing for the production of prosthetic limbs for those affected in their communities.

Refer to information on pages 2 and 3 of the Resource Booklet. [*14]
questions.markscheme_text:
Level 4 (12–14 marks): Comprehensive understanding of social, moral, and ethical implications of 3D printing prosthetics in developing countries. All three areas considered with both positive and negative perspectives. Well-developed, logically structured argument using Resource Booklet data and design knowledge.
Level 3 (9–11 marks): Good understanding of social/moral/ethical implications. At least two areas considered with balanced views.
Level 2 (5–8 marks): Sufficient understanding covering at least one area with some structure.
Level 1 (1–4 marks): Limited descriptive knowledge without evaluation.

Indicative Content:
• Social Implications: Restores mobility and dignity; allows individuals to walk without crutches, freeing their hands to carry water/food and perform productive work; reduces community dependency; reintegration into social activities and sports (e.g. wheelchair/prosthetic basketball); risk of social stigma or being ostracised if aesthetic appearance is strange or culturally unaccepted.
• Moral Implications: Moral duty to alleviate suffering and restore human potential; designer responsibility for biomechanical safety, structural durability, and avoiding stump skin ulceration/infection; managing expectations when simple mechanical prosthetics cannot match biological limb dexterity.
• Ethical Implications: Resource allocation and equity (who decides which amputees receive prosthetics in impoverished refugee camps?); cost and long-term funding (£2800 printer vs £20 per limb); lifespan and replacement protocols as child amputees grow; provision of physiotherapist rehabilitation and clinical follow-up; intellectual property of open-source CAD prosthetics vs medical certification standards.

questions.summary: Propose an alternative manufacturing process, thermoplastic material, and finishing techniques for an individual upper limb socket.
questions.prompt:
Page 2 of the Resource Booklet explains how a prosthetic specialist produces a positive model of a patient’s affected limb. This positive model is then used to create the socket of the prosthetic leg shown in Fig. 1 of the Resource Booklet.

Other than 3D printing, explain using sketches and/or notes a suitable manufacturing process which could be used to make the upper limb socket for an individual as shown in Fig. 1 of the Resource Booklet.

In your response you must include:
• technical details of methods of manufacture;
• appropriate materials and their properties;
• manufacturing processes to appropriately finish the socket. [14]
questions.markscheme_text:
Level 4 (11–14 marks): Excellent, end-to-end account of the manufacturing process for an upper limb socket covering all three bullet points. Naming a suitable thermoplastic (e.g. Polypropylene, Polyethylene, Polyurethane, ABS, HIPS) with property justification for custom one-off production. Clear annotated sketches and notes.
Level 3 (7–10 marks): Good account covering at least two bullet points with clear material and process choices.
Level 2 (4–6 marks): Sufficient account with basic material identification but limited one-off production justification.
Level 1 (1–3 marks): Basic account with knowledge gaps.

Indicative Content:
• Manufacturing Methods:
- Vacuum Forming / Drape Thermoforming: Highly suited for custom one-off manufacture over the plaster/vermiculite positive limb cast. A sheet of thermoplastic is clamped, heated by infrared ceramic heaters until pliable/rubbery, draped over the positive mould, and vacuum suction draws the sheet into intimate contact. Low tooling cost and quick cycle time.
- Thermoplastic Dip/Press Moulding: Alternatively, heated sheet pulled and seamed around mould.
- (If Injection Moulding is chosen): Must explain machine operation (hopper, reciprocating screw, heater bands, molten injection under pressure), but candidate must address that high tooling cost is normally unsuitable for one-off bespoke items unless modular cavity inserts are utilized.
• Materials & Properties:
- Polypropylene (PP): High fatigue resistance (living hinge property), low density, ductile, excellent chemical resistance, thermoforms easily over plaster positive.
- Polyurethane (PU) / TPU: Flexible, tear-resistant, resilient cushioning, skin-compatible, provides comfortable pressure distribution.
- High-Density Polyethylene (HDPE): Tough, lightweight, moisture resistant, easily trimmed.
• Finishing Processes:
- Trimming excess flash and flashing lines with oscillating cast cutter / bandsaw.
- Deburring and beveling socket rim edges with a rotary burr/flap wheel to prevent skin chaffing.
- Flaming or solvent polishing perimeter edges to create smooth, hygienic radius.
- Adding closed-cell foam liner (Plastazote) and adjustable hook-and-loop (Velcro) suspension straps.

questions.question: 3(a)
questions.summary: Calculate angle C formed between the tie and the forearm in the prosthetic arm force diagram.
questions.prompt:
Engineers have been working on a 3D-printed prosthetic arm which is easy to manufacture and simple to use. The design is shown in Fig. 4 of the Resource Booklet. It has a loose elbow joint which is held at a fixed 90° angle by a tie attached between the upper arm and the forearm. Fig. 5 shows a force diagram for the 3D-printed prosthetic arm.

In Fig. 5, the tie is anchored at a height of 120 mm above the elbow joint on the upper arm, and attached to the forearm at a distance of 70 mm from the elbow joint.

Calculate the angle C in Fig. 5 formed between the tie and the forearm. Show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 3 marks as follows:
• Correct trigonometry formula: tan(C) = Opposite / Adjacent ⇒ C = tan⁻¹(Opp / Adj) (1 mark)
• Correct substitution: C = tan⁻¹(120 / 70) = tan⁻¹(1.714) (1 mark)
• Calculate angle C: C = 59.68° (Accept rounded answers to 60° or 59.7°) (1 mark)
(Full marks if correct answer is given without working. ECF applies.)

questions.question: 3(b)
questions.summary: Calculate the length of the support tie to the nearest mm using trigonometry or Pythagoras.
questions.prompt: Calculate the length of the tie in Fig. 5 to the nearest mm. Show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 3 marks as follows:
• Method 1 (Trigonometry):
y = Opposite / sin(C) = 120 / sin(59.68°) = 120 / 0.8632 = 139 mm (3 marks)
• Method 2 (Pythagoras theorem):
y² = 120² + 70² = 14,400 + 4,900 = 19,300 (1 mark)
y = √19,300 = 138.92 mm (1 mark)
Rounding to nearest mm: y = 139 mm (1 mark)
(Full marks if correct answer 139 mm is given without working out. ECF applies.)

questions.question: 3(c)
questions.summary: Calculate the tensile force F in the tie under maximum hand load considering moments about the elbow joint.
questions.prompt:
Fig. 5 of the Resource Booklet shows a force diagram for the 3D-printed prosthetic arm.

Using the product information from Fig. 6 in the Resource Booklet:
• Mass of lower arm = 2 kg (acting at center of gravity distance 115 mm from elbow)
• Maximum recommended load held in hand = 9 kg (acting at distance 70 + 160 = 230 mm from elbow)
• Tie attached at 70 mm from elbow at angle C = 59.68°
• Gravitational field strength g = 9.81 N·kg⁻¹

Calculate the tensile force (F) in the tie when the maximum recommended load is being held in the hand.
You will find it useful to consider the moments acting about the elbow joint. Show your working. [6]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award 6 marks as follows:
• Hand load force L: 9 kg × 9.81 = 88.29 N (1 mark)
• Arm weight force W: 2 kg × 9.81 = 19.62 N (1 mark)
• Anticlockwise moments about elbow joint:
M_ACW = (L × 230 mm) + (W × 115 mm) = (88.29 × 230) + (19.62 × 115) = 20,306.7 + 2,256.3 = 22,563 N·mm (1 mark)
• Clockwise moment about elbow joint from tie force F:
Perpendicular component of F = F sin(C)
M_CW = F sin(59.68°) × 70 mm (1 mark)
• Equate moments in equilibrium (ΣM = 0):
22,563 = F × sin(59.68°) × 70 (1 mark)
F = 22,563 / (0.8632 × 70) = 22,563 / 60.426 = 373.4 N (allow 373 N to 374 N) (1 mark)
(Full marks if correct answer in range 373–374 N is given without working. ECF applies.)

questions.summary: Design mechanical and electronic solutions for the Endo-wrist forceps: 3:1 linear-to-oscillating amplification and forceps rotation.
questions.prompt:
The design engineers have been challenged to further develop the Endo-wrist described on page 5 of the Resource Booklet. They have identified that the current movement of the Endo-wrist does not sufficiently fulfil the movements of a surgeon’s hand and wrist, specifically when the Endo-wrist is being used with a forceps attachment as shown in Fig. 10 of the Resource Booklet.

Use sketches and/or notes to determine suitable technical solutions that overcome the following problems identified by the design engineers:

Problem 1: Opening and closing of forceps using the existing linear actuator (converting 5 mm linear stroke into 15 mm oscillating jaw tip opening — a 3:1 movement amplification).
Problem 2: Rotation of forceps (providing controllable continuous or bidirectional rotation of the forceps assembly).

In your response you must include details that demonstrate:
• appropriate mechanical function;
• appropriate electronic control systems;
• materials and components to be used. [14]
questions.markscheme_text:
Level 4 (11–14 marks): Candidate designs a suitable system producing the required motion for BOTH problems, covering all three bullet points. Excellent understanding of medical tool kinematics, explicit 3:1 amplification calculations/dimensions (5 mm stroke to 15 mm tip opening), clear annotated sketches, actuator selection, and biocompatible sterilizable materials.
Level 3 (7–10 marks): Suitable system solving both problems with clear sketches and notes, but minor gaps in dimensions or amplification calculations.
Level 2 (4–6 marks): Solves one problem or omits 3:1 amplification.
Level 1 (1–3 marks): Basic ideas with missing kinematics or unfeasible mechanics.

Indicative Content:
• Problem 1 (Forceps Jaw Motion & 3:1 Amplification):
- Conversion of linear actuator stroke (5 mm) to jaw tip oscillation (15 mm opening).
- Linkage mechanism: Scissor linkage, bell-crank lever, or toggle mechanism with pivot lever arm ratio of 3:1 (e.g. input arm 10 mm from pivot to actuator clevis, output jaw arm 30 mm from pivot to tip).
- Plain miniature ceramic/PTFE sleeve bearings to minimize friction and prevent biological fluid contamination.
- Biocompatible materials: Surgical grade stainless steel (316L) or titanium alloy (Ti-6Al-4V) suitable for autoclave steam sterilization or gamma irradiation.
• Problem 2 (Forceps Rotation & Transducer Control):
- Miniature rotational actuator: Brushless DC micromotor or stepper motor fitted with planetary reduction gearbox, mounted concentrically within the surgical shaft.
- Electronic control: Microcontroller receives rotary encoder input from surgeon's master console joystick/wheel; drives motor via H-bridge PWM motor driver (or microstepping driver for discrete angular positioning).
- Slip ring or flexible spiral ribbon cable to transmit signals through rotating joint without wire entanglement.
- Speed and position feedback: Closed-loop Hall-effect sensors or magnetic absolute encoder to guarantee sub-millimeter surgical accuracy and torque limiting.

questions.summary: Extended synoptic evaluation: How technological advancements have assisted design engineers to progress medical science.
questions.prompt:
Advancements in medical technology are one of the pioneering areas of design engineering.

Critically evaluate how technological advancements have assisted design engineers in the design and development of products to progress medical science.

You may refer to any of the products outlined in the Resource Booklet and also other products with which you are familiar. [*16]
questions.markscheme_text:
Level 4 (13–16 marks): Comprehensive synoptic evaluation of how technological advancements have assisted design engineers to progress medical science. Seamlessly synthesizes evidence from the Resource Booklet (3D-printed limbs, da Vinci surgical robotics, Endo-wrist) with wider engineering knowledge (CAD/CAM, FEA, CT/MRI scan slicing, bio-materials, VR/AR surgical training). Flawlessly structured, logical argument with clear evidence.
Level 3 (9–12 marks): Good understanding connecting technological advances to medical product development with substantiated examples.
Level 2 (5–8 marks): Sufficient understanding covering technological points with basic structure.
Level 1 (1–4 marks): Descriptive summary with limited evaluation.

Indicative Content:
• Rapid Prototyping & Additive Manufacturing:
- Evolution from SLA, SLS to direct metal laser sintering (DMLS/SLM) of titanium bone implants.
- Patient-specific customization: Converting 3D CT/MRI DICOM scans directly into STL surface meshes to 3D print bespoke cranial plates, hearing aids, dental bridges, and burn-victim skin scaffolds.
- Rapid turnaround and drastic cost reduction (£2800 printer yielding £20 prosthetic limbs vs traditional £1000s plaster casting in developing countries).
• Digital Engineering Tools (CAD, CAE, FEA, AR/VR):

• Robotic Surgery & Tele-operation:

- Miniaturization: 1 cm diameter instruments reducing incision size (minimally invasive keyhole surgery), dramatically decreasing tissue trauma, hospital stay, infection risk, and recovery time.
• Smart Materials & Micro-electronics:
- High-precision micro-actuators, piezoelectric ultrasonic scalpels, wireless real-time endoscopic cameras, and bio-inert polymers.

questions.question: 1(a)
questions.summary: Identify three ways in which the manufacturer of the home lift can ensure safe operation by its users.
questions.prompt:
Fig. 1.1 shows an electrically-powered home lift. The first image shows the lift on the ground floor. The second image shows the lift on the upper floor.

Identify three ways in which the manufacturer of the home lift can ensure the safe operation of the lift by its users. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
One mark for identifying each of three ways in which the manufacturer can ensure safe operation (max 3 marks):
• Provide safety warning labels (e.g. maximum load 2 people / 350 kg) (1)
• Door interlock mechanism to prevent lift moving if door is open (1)
• Overweight load sensor and audible alarm (1)
• Key lock or PIN pad to prevent children operating the lift unsupervised (1)
• Battery backup system to lower carriage safely in case of power failure (1)
• Emergency stop button / alarm button to summon assistance (1)
• Sensitive safety edges on car underside to stop motor if an obstruction is met (1)

questions.question: 1(b)(i)
questions.summary: Calculate the time in seconds for the lift to rise 2800 mm at a speed of 0.08 m/s.
questions.prompt:
The home lift in Fig. 1.1 uses a screw thread and nut mechanism in which the nut is attached to the lift and rotated through a double chain drive by an electric motor. The screw thread is held in position and does not move. Fig. 1.2 shows the mechanism.

The lift moves at a speed of \(0.08\text{ m s}^{-1}\).

Calculate the time taken in seconds (s) for the lift to rise between floors which are \(2800\text{ mm}\) apart. Show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award three marks as follows:
• Rearranging speed formula: \(\text{Time} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}\) (1)
• Converting distance units: \(2800\text{ mm} = 2.8\text{ m}\) (1)
• Calculating time: \(\text{Time} = \frac{2.8}{0.08} = 35\text{ s}\) (1)

questions.question: 1(b)(ii)
questions.summary: Calculate the required motor rotational speed in rpm for the nut to climb the thread at 0.08 m/s.
questions.prompt: Analysing the data in Fig. 1.2 (screw thread \(8\text{ mm}\) pitch, motor sprockets \(20\) teeth, nut sprockets \(30\) teeth), calculate the motor rotational speed required in revolutions per minute (rpm) to cause the nut to climb up the thread at a speed of \(0.08\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award three marks as follows:
• In 1 second, nut linear travel \(= 0.08\text{ m} = 80\text{ mm}\). Nut rev/s \(= \frac{80\text{ mm}}{8\text{ mm pitch}} = 10\text{ rev/s}\) (1)
• Sprocket gear ratio \(= \frac{\text{driven}}{\text{driver}} = \frac{30}{20} = 1.5\). Motor rev/s \(= 10 \times 1.5 = 15\text{ rev/s}\) (1)
• Convert to rpm: \(15 \times 60 = 900\text{ rpm}\) (1)
(OR: Nut rpm \(= 10 \times 60 = 600\text{ rpm}\); Motor rpm \(= 600 \times 1.5 = 900\text{ rpm}\))

questions.question: 1(b)(iii)
questions.summary: Give two reasons why a double chain drive is used in this home lift application.
questions.prompt: Give two reasons why a double chain drive is used in this application. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
One mark for each of two valid reasons (max 2 marks):
• Redundancy / safety: if one chain breaks, the second chain continues to hold and drive the carriage, preventing system failure (1)
• Load distribution: splitting the drive torque across two chains halves the tension in each link (1)
• Compactness: allows two narrower chains instead of one bulky single chain, reducing required motor enclosure depth (1)
• Positive non-slip drive: roller chains cannot slip under peak starting inertia unlike friction belt drives (1)

questions.question: 1(b)(iv)
questions.summary: Calculate the power required in watts to raise a 350 kg lift at 0.08 m/s.
questions.prompt:
The maximum total mass of the lift and occupants is \(350\text{ kg}\).

Calculate the power required in watts (W) to raise the \(350\text{ kg}\) lift at a velocity of \(0.08\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Show your working.

\(\text{gravitational potential energy} = mgh\)
\(\text{power} = \frac{E}{t}\)
\(\text{gravitational field strength, } g = 9.81\text{ N kg}^{-1}\) [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award three marks as follows:
• Method 1: In \(t = 1\text{ s}\), lift rises \(h = 0.08\text{ m}\) (1)
\(E = mgh = 350 \times 9.81 \times 0.08 = 274.68\text{ J}\) (1)
\(P = \frac{E}{t} = \frac{274.68}{1} = 274.68\text{ W}\) (allow \(275\text{ W}\)) (1)
• Method 2: \(F = mg = 350 \times 9.81 = 3433.5\text{ N}\) (1)
\(P = F \times v = 3433.5 \times 0.08 = 274.68\text{ W}\) (2)

questions.question: 1(b)(v)
questions.summary: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using a screw thread and nut mechanism in a lift.
questions.prompt:
Conventional lifts usually use a cable mechanism with an electric motor located at the top of the lift shaft.

Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using a screw thread and nut mechanism in a lift. [4]
questions.markscheme_text:
Up to 2 marks for explaining an advantage (1 mark for point, 1 mark for application context):
• Self-locking: the high friction inherent in screw threads prevents back-driving, meaning the carriage cannot free-fall even if motor power or brakes fail (2)
• No overhead motor room: the mechanism mounts behind or underneath the car, eliminating the need for rooftop machinery housings (2)
• No cable stretch: leadscrew drive maintains precise floor levelling over years without cable stretch adjustment (2)

Up to 2 marks for explaining a disadvantage:
• Low efficiency / speed: substantial sliding friction between nut and thread requires more motor energy and limits ascent speed (2)
• High maintenance lubrication: screw thread requires regular grease maintenance to prevent excessive friction, wear, and noise (2)
• Limited travel height: long screws are susceptible to buckling and whipping at high rotation, limiting maximum floor heights (2)

questions.question: 1(c)

questions.question: 2(a)
questions.summary: Calculate the maximum straight part length which can be shipped in a 305 x 215 x 100 mm box.

Calculate the maximum straight part length which can be shipped in this cardboard box. Give your answer in mm to 1 decimal place and show your working. [3]

questions.question: 2(b)(i)

questions.question: 2(b)(ii)
questions.summary: Calculate the mass in grams of the turned brass part (cylinder plus cone).
questions.prompt:
Calculate the mass in grams (g) of the part shown in Fig. 2.2. Give your answer to 1 decimal place and show your working.

\(\text{Area of a circle} = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}\)
\(\text{Volume of a cone} = \frac{1}{3} \times \text{base area} \times \text{height}\)
\(\text{Density of brass} = 8.73\text{ g cm}^{-3}\) [5]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award five marks as follows:
• Cone volume: \(V_{\text{cone}} = \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{\pi \times 26^2}{4} \times 20 = 3539.53\text{ mm}^3\) (1)
• Cylinder volume: \(V_{\text{cyl}} = \frac{\pi \times 26^2}{4} \times 15 = 7963.94\text{ mm}^3\) (1)
• Total volume: \(V = 7963.94 + 3539.53 = 11503.47\text{ mm}^3\) (1)
• Volume conversion to cm³: \(\frac{11503.47}{1000} = 11.5035\text{ cm}^3\) (1)

questions.question: 2(b)(iii)
questions.summary: Calculate the volume in mm³ of waste brass generated when turning the part from bar stock.
questions.prompt:
The part in Fig. 2.2 is to be turned on a centre lathe from a cylindrical brass bar with diameter \(30\text{ mm}\) and length \(35\text{ mm}\).

Calculate the volume in \(\text{mm}^3\) of the waste brass generated. Give your answer to 1 decimal place and show your working. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award two marks as follows:
• Original bar volume: \(V_{\text{bar}} = \frac{\pi \times 30^2}{4} \times 35 = 24740.04\text{ mm}^3\) (1)
• Waste volume \(= V_{\text{bar}} - V_{\text{part}} = 24740.04 - 11503.47 = 13236.5\text{ mm}^3\) (1) (allow ECF from 2(b)(ii))

questions.question: 2(b)(iv)
questions.summary: Calculate the minimum allowable diameter for 26.00 mm with a tolerance of ±2%.
questions.prompt:
The diameter of the part must be \(26.00\text{ mm}\) with a tolerance of \(\pm 2\%\).

Calculate the minimum allowable diameter in mm of the part. Show your working. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award two marks as follows:
• Tolerance calculation: \(26.00 \times 0.02 = 0.52\text{ mm}\) (1)
• Minimum diameter: \(26.00 - 0.52 = 25.48\text{ mm}\) (1)

questions.question: 2(c)
questions.summary: Calculate the initial velocity for a tennis ball to reach 2.5 m vertically using v² = u² + 2as.
questions.prompt:
A machine is being developed to help tennis players practise their serve. The machine projects a tennis ball vertically to a height, \(s\), of \(2.5\text{ m}\).

Use the formula, \(v^2 = u^2 + 2as\), to calculate the initial velocity, \(u\), at which the ball needs to leave the machine so that it just reaches the required height of \(2.5\text{ m}\). Give your answer in \(\text{m s}^{-1}\) and show your working.

Acceleration, \(a\), due to gravity in this situation is \(-9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}\) [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award two marks as follows:
• Stating that final vertical velocity at peak height is zero: \(v = 0\) (1)
• Substituting and solving: \(0 = u^2 + 2(-9.81)(2.5) \implies u^2 = 49.05 \implies u = \sqrt{49.05} = 7.0\text{ m s}^{-1}\) (1)

questions.question: 3(a)
questions.summary: Discuss the implications to manufacturers of producing BSI Kitemark approved products.

To certify that products conform to a standard set by the British Standards Institute (BSI), many products carry the BSI Kitemark® shown in Fig. 3.

questions.question: 4(a)
questions.summary: Identify two issues associated with providing power to the robotic lawnmower charging station.

Identify two issues associated with providing power to the charging station. [2]

questions.question: 4(b)(i)
questions.summary: Describe how rigidity of the polymer part in Fig. 4.2a and 4.2b is achieved through effective design.

The case of the robotic lawnmower is made from a thermo softening polymer.

Fig. 4.2a and Fig. 4.2b show two views of a typical thermo softening polymer part from a similar garden product.

questions.question: 4(b)(ii)

questions.question: 4(b)(iii)

questions.question: 4(d)
questions.summary: Complete the system diagram for the robotic lawnmower including inputs, microcontroller, and outputs.

The robotic lawnmower is controlled by an electronic system with a number of sensors, user-operated controls and outputs. The robotic lawnmower function is described below:

questions.question: 4(e)(i)
questions.summary: Calculate the voltage at point VA when the battery voltage is 10.5 V in the potential divider.
questions.prompt:
Fig. 4.3 shows a circuit diagram for the part of the robotic lawnmower which monitors the battery voltage.

The lithium ion battery produces a nominal voltage of \(11.1\text{ V}\). When the battery voltage drops to \(10.5\text{ V}\) an alert is generated within the microcontroller code and the robotic lawnmower returns to its charging station.

Calculate the voltage (V) at point \(V_A\) in Fig. 4.3 when the battery voltage is \(10.5\text{ V}\). Give your answer to 2 decimal places and show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award three marks as follows:
• Potential divider formula / Ohm's law: \(V_A = V_{\text{in}} \times \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\) (1)
• Substitution: \(V_A = 10.5 \times \frac{1.8}{3.9 + 1.8} = 10.5 \times \frac{1.8}{5.7}\) (1)
• Calculation: \(V_A = 3.3158\text{ V} = 3.32\text{ V}\) (to 2 d.p.) (1)

questions.question: 4(e)(ii)
questions.summary: Calculate the 10-bit ADC value produced when the input voltage VA is 3.32 V.

Voltage \(V_A\) in Fig. 4.3 is fed into an analogue to digital converter (ADC) pin on the microcontroller. The ADC produces a full-scale value of 1023 when the analogue input is \(5.0\text{ V}\).

Calculate the ADC value produced when the input voltage \(V_A\) is at the value you calculated in part (e)(i) (\(3.32\text{ V}\)). Give your answer as a rounded-down integer and show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award three marks as follows:
• Voltage fraction: \(\frac{3.32}{5.0} = 0.664\) (1)
• ADC scaling: \(0.664 \times 1023 = 679.272\) (1)

questions.summary: Discuss design engineering considerations for developing a new groundwater pump for a remote rural village.
questions.prompt:
Water scarcity is a major concern for parts of the developing world. The World Health Organisation (WHO) is one organisation that is helping by fitting water pumps to extract groundwater in those rural areas worst affected.

Discuss the issues that a design engineer would need to consider when developing a new water pump for use in a remote rural village.

Refer to information on pages 2, 3 and 4 of the Resource Booklet. [*14]
questions.markscheme_text:
Level 4 (11–14 marks): Comprehensive discussion of a wide range (at least 3) of issues a design engineer must consider when developing a new water pump for a remote village. Effectively exemplifies points using Resource Booklet data. Well-constructed, logically structured narrative with supported evaluative comments.
Level 3 (7–10 marks): Good critical discussion covering at least 2 issues with mostly effective use of Resource Booklet evidence.
Level 2 (4–6 marks): Sufficient understanding covering at least 2 issues with basic structure.
Level 1 (1–3 marks): Limited discussion; basic isolated points without evaluation.

Indicative Content:
• Operating Environment & Climate: Arid equatorial conditions with extreme high temperatures (up to 41°C) and tropical monsoons where surface runoff rapidly evaporates or is contaminated; must be installable on unprepared waste land or shared communal ground.
• Location & Transport Distance: Wells often located between multiple villages to share drilling and setup costs; requires villagers (primarily women and young children) to walk miles carrying water, increasing exhaustion, school absence, loss of economic productivity, and vulnerability to violence.
• Water Source Quality & Geology: Deep groundwater (>10m) is naturally filtered through soil layers against surface pathogens/faeces, but may contain dissolved heavy metals or bacteria from leaking septic systems; requires regular testing which rural areas lack financial and technical resources to perform.
• Materials & Manufacturing: Cast alloy main body provides high corrosion resistance and long operational lifespan in harsh outdoor weather; minimal moving parts to simplify sand/die casting and machining; balance between initial material cost and ruggedness.
• Maintenance & Supply Chain: Moving parts need periodic lubrication; rubber/nitrile piston seals wear out over time; seals and lubricants must be cheap and easily sourced locally without prolonged shipping delays causing well shutdown.
• Ergonomics & Human Factors: Handle height, fulcrum pivot distance, and effort required to operate the lever arm (India MkIII has 650 mm handle vs 150 mm lever arm) must suit the anthropometrics and physical strength of women and children who collect the majority of water.

questions.summary: Calculate the number of complete pump handle cycles required to fill a 20-litre container with water.

Using the information on page 5 of the Resource Booklet, calculate how many complete cycles of the pump handle will be required to fill one 20 litre container with water. Show your working.

The formula for calculating the volume of a cylinder is $V = \pi r^2 h$. [6]
questions.markscheme_text:
Full Credit Method (accounting for Piston Rod volume, max 6 marks):
• Cylinder dimensions from Fig. 5: Diameter $d = 100\text{ mm} \implies r = 50\text{ mm} = 0.05\text{ m}$; Stroke $h = 300\text{ mm} = 0.3\text{ m}$.
• Piston rod dimensions: Diameter $D = 38\text{ mm} \implies R = 19\text{ mm} = 0.019\text{ m}$.
• Gross cylinder volume: $V_{\text{cyl}} = \pi r^2 h = \pi \times (0.05)^2 \times 0.3 = 0.002356\text{ m}^3 = 2356\text{ cm}^3 = 2.356\text{ L}$ (or $2.365\text{ L}$ using truncated values).
• Piston rod displaced volume: $V_{\text{rod}} = \pi R^2 h = \pi \times (0.019)^2 \times 0.3 = 0.000340\text{ m}^3 = 340\text{ cm}^3 = 0.34\text{ L}$ (or $0.30\text{ L}$).
• Net water displaced per stroke: $V_{\text{net}} = V_{\text{cyl}} - V_{\text{rod}} = 2.365 - 0.30 = 2.065\text{ L}$ (or $2.1\text{ L}$).
• Number of cycles required: $\text{Cycles} = 20 / 2.065 \approx 9.68$ (or $20 / 2.1 = 9.52$).
• Round up to complete cycles: 10 complete cycles.

Alternative Method (ignoring Piston Rod, max 4 marks):
• $V = 2.365\text{ L} \implies \text{Cycles} = 20 / 2.365 = 8.45 \implies$ 9 complete cycles.

questions.summary: Calculate the minimum number of RB500 photovoltaic panels required to produce 1890 kWh annual energy output.
questions.prompt:
A design team is investigating whether the use of a solar-powered water pump would be more of a viable solution.

It is looking into the use of the RB500 photovoltaic panels shown in Fig. 6 of the Resource Booklet. A number of these panels could be used together in a photovoltaic array to provide the required energy output.

It has been determined that an annual energy output of 1890 kilowatt-hours (kWh) is required for the pump to work efficiently.

Calculate the minimum number of photovoltaic panels of the type shown that would be required to produce the energy output needed for the water pump.

Use the equation below and information on page 6 of the Resource Booklet. Show your working.

$$E = A \times r \times H \times PR$$
Where:
• $E$ = annual energy output from photovoltaic array (kWh)
• $A$ = total photovoltaic array area (m²)
• $r$ = photovoltaic panel yield
• $H$ = annual average solar irradiation (kWh m⁻²)
• $PR$ = performance ratio, coefficient of losses. [6]
questions.markscheme_text:
Mark Scheme Steps (6 marks):
1. Rearrange formula in terms of $A$: $A = \frac{E}{r \times H \times PR}$ [1 mark]
2. Extract correct data from Resource Booklet (page 6):
- $r = 0.15$
- $PR = 0.75$
- $H = 2100\text{ kWh m}^{-2}$ [2 marks]
3. Substitute values and calculate total area $A$:
$$A = \frac{1890}{0.15 \times 2100 \times 0.75} = \frac{1890}{236.25} = 8.0\text{ m}^2\text{ [1 mark]}$$
4. Calculate surface area of single RB500 panel:
$$\text{Area} = 1.0\text{ m} \times 0.5\text{ m} = 0.5\text{ m}^2\text{ [1 mark]}$$
5. Divide total array area by single panel area:
$$\text{Panels} = \frac{8\text{ m}^2}{0.5\text{ m}^2} = \mathbf{16\text{ panels}}\text{ [1 mark]}$$

Level 2 (4–6 marks): Sufficient understanding with basic points.
Level 1 (1–3 marks): Limited description without evaluation.

Indicative Content:
• Stakeholder Considerations (WHO, NGOs, Government, Donors, Maintenance Teams):
- High initial capital outlay for 16 PV panels, inverters, motor controllers, and structural mounting arrays compared to inexpensive manual hand pumps.

- Maintenance: While PV cells have no moving parts, dust, sand, and bird droppings rapidly degrade panel yield in arid zones, requiring regular cleaning; electronics/inverters can fail under extreme heat (up to 41°C).
- Security risks: High-value solar panels and copper wiring are prone to theft and vandalism; necessitates fencing, locking fasteners, or community guarding.
- Energy storage / multi-use potential: Excess electricity generated during peak midday solar irradiance can be stored in batteries or used to power community lighting, refrigeration for medicine, or phone charging.
- Need for manual backup: If electrical components fail or during extended monsoon overcast periods, a manual hand-pump mechanism must remain operational.
• User Considerations (Villagers, Women, Children):

- Faster water delivery: Motorized pumping fills 20L containers rapidly, drastically shortening queues at the well.
- Social & educational benefits: Frees young girls and women from daily water collection chores, enabling girls to attend school and women to pursue trade/farming.
- Operational education: Villagers must be trained to operate taps and valves responsibly, avoiding leaving taps running and wasting depleted groundwater reserves.

questions.summary: Technical design solutions: PICAXE solar-tracking microcontroller flowchart/code (Issue 1) and a 32:1 compound spur gear train (Issue 2).
questions.prompt:
A decision has been made to proceed with the design of the solar-powered water pump.
The design team has been given two immediate issues to overcome.

Issue 1
The efficiency of the photovoltaic array will vary throughout the day depending on the position of the sun in the sky. In order to improve the efficiency it has been suggested that the photovoltaic array should move so that it always faces the sun.
A system has been designed to do this which uses a motor, connected through a gearbox, to move the array. The system is controlled by a PICAXE microcontroller. Page 7 of the Resource Booklet explains the operation of the system.
A program flowchart or code with annotation is required for the PICAXE microcontroller so that the photovoltaic array will move to follow the sun across the sky.

Issue 2
Spur gears need to be used for the gearbox to move the photovoltaic array.
A gear ratio of 32:1 is required.
Due to the remote area it is working in, the design team has a limited selection of spur gears available shown on page 7 of the Resource Booklet.
A gear system is required using only the available spur gears that would produce the required gear ratio.

Use sketches and/or notes to determine suitable technical solutions that overcome the two issues identified. All of the information you need is on page 7 of the Resource Booklet. [16]
questions.markscheme_text:
Issue 1 (8 marks) – Microcontroller Flowchart / Code:
• Identification of inputs: Two LDR potential dividers connected to analogue ADC inputs C.0 and C.2.
• Reading ADC values: Use of `readadc c.0, varA` and `readadc c.2, varB` (or `readadc c.0, LDR1` / `readadc c.2, LDR2`).
• Comparison logic:
- If $LDR_1 = LDR_2$ (balanced light): Hold motor (`Low B.0`, `Low B.1`).
- If $LDR_1 < LDR_2$: Turn motor Clockwise (`High B.0`, `Low B.1`).
- If $LDR_1 > LDR_2$: Turn motor Counter-Clockwise (`Low B.0`, `High B.1`).
• Motor driver control: Correct dual output pins (B.0 and B.1) driving L293D H-bridge IC.
• Program loop: Unconditional jump (`goto main`) ensuring continuous closed-loop sun tracking.

Issue 2 (8 marks) – 32:1 Gearbox Design:
• Gear ratio formula: $\text{Gear Ratio} = \frac{\text{Product of Driven Teeth}}{\text{Product of Driver Teeth}} = 32:1$.
• Identification that a compound gear train is required because a single pair ratio of 32:1 would require a 5-tooth pinion ($160 / 32 = 5$), which does not exist in stock.
• Factoring 32 into two stages: $32 = 8 \times 4$ (or $4 \times 8$).
• Available gears in inventory: 160t (2), 80t (3), 40t (2), 20t (3).
• Stage 1 (4:1 reduction): Driver 20t meshing with Driven 80t ($80 / 20 = 4:1$).
• Stage 2 (8:1 reduction): The 80t gear shares a common shaft with a second 20t driver pinion, which meshes with a 160t driven gear on the array output shaft ($160 / 20 = 8:1$).
• Total Compound Ratio: $\frac{80 \times 160}{20 \times 20} = 4 \times 8 = \mathbf{32:1}$.
• Inventory check: Uses two 20t gears (3 in stock), one 80t gear (3 in stock), and one 160t gear (2 in stock).
• Annotated schematic showing input motor shaft, intermediate compound shaft, output turntable shaft, and gear tooth counts.

questions.summary: Critically evaluate the DLR-90 industrial trolley for transporting 20L water containers and suggest design improvements.
questions.prompt:
During the course of a day the average family will require two containers of water of the type shown in Fig. 10 of the Resource Booklet. Traditionally, these are collected by the women and children of the families and are sometimes carried over large distances.

The WHO is working with a company that specialises in producing heavy-duty trollies for industrial applications. The company has proposed a trolley design shown in Fig. 11 of the Resource Booklet that could be used by families to transport water from the water source to their homes.

Critically evaluate the design of the trolley in Fig. 11 of the Resource Booklet making suggestions for improvement for the task specified. [*14]
questions.markscheme_text:
Level 4 (11–14 marks): Comprehensive evaluation of the DLR-90 industrial trolley design with detailed, justified recommendations for improvement. Product analysis consistently aligned with the task of carrying two 20L water containers across remote rural terrain by women and children. Information in Resource Booklet fully exploited. Logically structured narrative.
Level 3 (7–10 marks): Good evaluation covering trolley materials, wheels, bed dimensions, and weight with several practical improvements.
Level 2 (4–6 marks): Sufficient evaluation with basic points.
Level 1 (1–3 marks): Limited descriptive comments without evaluation.

Indicative Content:
• Evaluation of Existing DLR-90 Trolley:
- Load Capacity: 90 kg max load is well suited for two 20L containers ($2 \times 20\text{ kg} = 40\text{ kg} + 10\text{ kg trolley} = 50\text{ kg}$ total load, safety factor ~1.8).
- Materials: Aluminium frame is lightweight and rust-free, but costly to produce and difficult to weld in rural villages; steel axle is robust but prone to corrosion in wet conditions and requires grease-packed sealed bearings.
- Wheel & Tyre Limitations: 150 mm diameter wheels are far too small for uneven, rutted dirt roads, mud, and sand; solid rubber tyres provide zero shock absorption, causing extreme jarring, spill risk, and operator fatigue.
- Carrying Bed Size: $380 \times 250\text{ mm}$ bed is smaller in depth than the container base ($280 \times 280\text{ mm}$), causing container overhang and tipping. The bed is too narrow to place two containers side-by-side ($2 \times 280 = 560\text{ mm} > 380\text{ mm}$), forcing vertical stacking which elevates the centre of gravity and causes rollover on slopes.
- ABS bed material is brittle under sharp impact on rocks.
• Recommended Design Improvements:
- Wheel Overhaul: Fit large diameter (300–400 mm) pneumatic or puncture-proof micro-cellular / airless tyres with wider tread to roll easily over rough terrain and soft sand.
- Bed Redesign: Widen and lengthen the carrying platform (at least $600 \times 300\text{ mm}$) to support two containers side-by-side with a low centre of gravity; add raised perimeter retaining lips, tie-down bungee straps, or a quick-release wire cage.
- Material & Chassis: Fabricate frame from tubular mild steel with galvanized or epoxy powder coating for lower cost, higher impact toughness, and easy repair by local blacksmiths.
- Ergonomic Handle: Ergonomic twin-loop push/pull handle with soft rubber grips; ensure telescoping adjustment mechanism has sealed detent pins to prevent grit/sand jamming.

\[ R = 1.25 \times \frac{0.003}{0.005 \times 50 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{0.00375}{2.5 \times 10^{-7}} = 15000\ \Omega \] (1)

Level 4 (11–14 marks): Comprehensive discussion/evaluation, information in the RB used effectively to fully exemplify points, well-developed and logically structured line of reasoning.

Indicative content:

questions.summary: Design a pulley drive from the flywheel to the TB-401/10 generator for 3 A charging, and an electronic system that switches off the output below 1000 rpm.
questions.prompt:
The designers of the rowing machine charging system described in Question 2 wish to develop a working prototype. A TB-401/10 generator (page 5 of the RB) converts the rower’s kinetic energy into electrical power. The average user produces 600 rpm at the flywheel. The prototype must charge the iPhone with the specification in Fig. 8.

Issue 1: A drive system is required to transfer the rotary motion from the flywheel to the generator at an appropriate speed.

Issue 2: Mobile devices require a 5 V output; the generator maintains 5 V only if its pulley rotates at a minimum of 1000 rpm. An annotated system diagram is required, describing an electronic system to monitor the speed of the generator pulley and to switch off the electrical output if the speed drops below 1000 rpm. Appropriate sensor(s) and output device(s) must be identified.

Use sketches and/or notes. All information is on pages 4 and 5 of the Resource Booklet. [16]
questions.markscheme_text:
Level 4 (13–16): Both solutions comprehensive and well developed; end-to-end process clear. Level 3 (9–12): Both covered, one may be underdeveloped. Level 2 (5–8): Both may be underdeveloped. Level 1 (1–4): Basic. (Max 8 marks per issue.)

Issue 1 – drive system:
• Required current (Fig. 8) = 3 A → Fig. 7 gives a generator speed of ≈1500 rpm (allow 1400–1600).
• Velocity ratio: $\frac{600}{1500} = 0.4$ (or $\frac{1500}{600} = 2.5$).
• $\frac{\text{driven } (50\text{ mm})}{\text{driver}} = 0.4 \Rightarrow$ driver pulley on flywheel $= \frac{50}{0.4} = \mathbf{125\text{ mm}}$.
• Workable drive detail: pulley and belt, attaching driver pulley to the flywheel, belt tensioning, ribbed belt to reduce slip, generator mounting (gears / friction wheel / chain and sprocket also allowed).

Issue 2 – speed-monitoring system:
• Sensor: slotted opto-switch with slotted disc on the pulley (or gear-tooth sensor, reed switch, microswitch, quadrature encoder).
• Signal: a stream of pulses whose frequency is proportional to speed.
• Process: microcontroller measures the time interval between pulses.
• Output: relay or MOSFET switching the charging current.
• Logic: if interval is shorter than the 1000 rpm threshold, output high → relay on → charging current flows; otherwise relay off. Add a short delay to stop rapid switching around 1000 rpm.

questions.question: 1(a)(ii)

questions.markscheme_text:

• Compact volume: High gear reduction in a small physical envelope allows a lightweight handheld tool.

questions.summary: Calculate the height h of the zip-line end point given a 2.8 m start, 30 m run, and 2.5 degree slope.
questions.prompt:

2. Calculate $y$: $y = 30 \times \tan(2.5^\circ) \approx 1.3099\text{ m}$ [1 mark]

questions.prompt:

Calculate the distance d in m. Give your answer to 2 decimal places and show your working. [4]
questions.markscheme_text:
Sine Rule Steps (4 marks):

2. Apply sine rule: $\frac{d}{\sin(66^\circ)} = \frac{3}{\sin(45^\circ)}$ [1 mark]
3. Rearrange: $d = \frac{3 \times \sin(66^\circ)}{\sin(45^\circ)}$ [1 mark]

questions.question: 2(c)(iii)
questions.summary: Calculate the probability of zip-line failure over a 25-year period (300 days/year, 1 in 25000 daily failure chance).
questions.prompt:
A risk assessment is carried out on the zip-line for the children’s play park. The assessment suggests there is a 1 in 25 000 chance of failure each day it is used.

Calculate the probability of failure over a 25-year period if the zip-line is used for 300 days per year.

Give your answer as a percentage and show your working. [4]
questions.markscheme_text:
Cumulative Probability Calculation (4 marks):
1. Daily probability of zero failure: $P(\text{no failure}) = 1 - \frac{1}{25\,000} = 0.99996$ [1 mark]
2. Total days of use: $n = 300 \times 25 = 7500\text{ days}$ [1 mark]
3. Probability of zero failure over 25 years: $(0.99996)^{7500} \approx 0.7408$ (or $0.74$) [1 mark]
4. Probability of at least one failure: $1 - 0.74 = 0.26 = \mathbf{26\%}$ (allow 25.9% to 26%) [1 mark]

Level 1 (1–3 marks): Limited descriptive comments.

Indicative Content:
• Pollution: Emissions of greenhouse gases ($CO_2$, $NO_x$, $SO_2$) leading to atmospheric warming, smog, and acid rain; chemical discharges and plastic pollution into aquatic ecosystems.
• Natural Resource Depletion: Unsustainable extraction of finite fossil fuels (oil, gas, coal), deforestation for industrial timber and agriculture, depletion of rare earth minerals (neodymium, lithium, cobalt) for consumer electronics.

questions.summary: Critically examine ways design engineers reduce environmental impacts of a chosen product across its 5 lifecycle stages.
questions.prompt:
Design engineers play an important role in the design of future technological products. They have the ability to minimise the negative impact that products have on the environment.
