questions.markscheme_text:
Level 4 (11–14 marks): Comprehensive critical evaluation of ways design engineers reduce environmental impacts across all 5 lifecycle stages with clear justifications and specific technical strategies.
Level 3 (7–10 marks): Good critical evaluation covering most lifecycle stages.
Level 2 (4–6 marks): Adequate evaluation covering some stages.
Level 1 (1–3 marks): Basic descriptive response.

Lifecycle Stages & Indicative Strategies:
• 1. Raw material extraction: Selecting sustainably sourced, renewable, or post-consumer recycled materials (e.g. bio-based polymers, recycled aluminium); reducing raw material mass via generative design.
• 2. Manufacture: Designing for minimal scrap / near-net-shape processing (injection moulding, additive manufacturing); reducing embedded energy and eliminating toxic solvents/finishes.
• 3. Distribution: Designing compact, flat-pack, or nested geometries to maximise shipping pallet density and minimise logistics fuel; replacing plastic packaging with biodegradable mycelium or pulp.
• 4. Use phase: Maximising operational energy efficiency (low-power microcontrollers, LED lighting, high thermal insulation); extending product durability via modular, easily replaceable wear components.
• 5. Disposal / End-of-Life: Design for Disassembly (DfD) using standard fasteners rather than permanent adhesives; moulding SPI polymer resin codes for rapid robotic sorting; establishing circular take-back schemes.

questions.summary: Determine technical solutions for The Snake WEC: 3:1 frequency multiplying reciprocating-to-rotary mechanism, and wireless telemetry microcontroller counter.
questions.prompt:
An engineering company is developing a wave energy converter (WEC) to generate renewable electricity from the kinetic energy of waves on the sea. The name given to the prototype WEC is ‘The Snake’.

The Snake WEC is described on pages 4 and 5 of the Resource Booklet. The Snake is a modular product aimed at entrepreneurs who are interested in venturing into the renewable energy industry.

The design engineers have two issues to overcome:
Issue 1: When on the sea, the movement of The Snake segments creates reciprocating motion of a pushrod shown in Fig. 4. A mechanical system is required to convert this input reciprocating motion into an output rotary motion to turn the generator axle and multiply the frequency by three (for each reciprocation, generator shaft rotates 3 times).
Issue 2: Each prototype unit will contain a microcontroller system to record the total number of pushrod reciprocations, to be collected via wireless technology by engineers in a boat. A system diagram and a program flowchart are required, showing how an identified sensor detects pushrod reciprocations, records count, and transmits data wirelessly.

Use sketches and/or notes to determine suitable technical solutions that overcome the two issues identified.

Refer to information on pages 4 and 5 of the Resource Booklet. [16]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award up to 8 marks for Issue 1 and up to 8 marks for Issue 2 (Total 16 marks):

Issue 1 Breakdown (8 marks):
• Reciprocating to Rotary conversion (4 marks): Rack and pinion mechanism or slider-crank / scotch yoke arrangement clearly sketched and annotated; bidirectional clutch / freewheel / one-way sprag bearing mechanism to maintain unidirectional rotation.
• 3:1 Frequency Multiplication (4 marks): Gear train with exact $3:1$ ratio (e.g. 60-tooth driver gear driving 20-tooth pinion, or 36T to 12T), or pulley/sprocket system with $3:1$ diameter ratio; correct gear meshing and axle bearings labelled.

Issue 2 Breakdown (8 marks):
• Sensor & System Diagram (3 marks): Identifies valid sensor (magnetic reed switch / Hall effect sensor with magnet on pushrod, optical interrupter, or limit microswitch); shows pushrod sensor inputting to microcontroller, outputting to wireless transmitter module (Bluetooth Low Energy, RF transceiver 433/868 MHz, or Wi-Fi).
• Program Flowchart / Logic (5 marks): Clear flowchart with Start block, initialising count `C = 0`, polling loop checking if sensor activated; debouncing delay/state check; incrementing counter `C = C + 1`; checking for wireless interrogation signal from boat; transmitting total count packet; looping back continually.

questions.question: 4(a)
questions.summary: Calculate Brinell Hardness Number (BHN) for F=10 kN, D=10 mm, Di=0.60 mm and evaluate pushrod suitability (3900-4100 MPa).
questions.prompt:
During the development of The Snake prototype WEC described on pages 4 and 5 of the Resource Booklet, the design engineers used destructive testing techniques on materials in order to check their properties.

They chose to use the Brinell Hardness Test which is described on page 6 of the Resource Booklet.

When one material was tested, the following results were obtained:
• Force applied $F = 10\text{ kN}$
• Indenter diameter $D = 10\text{ mm}$
• Indentation diameter $D_i = 0.60\text{ mm}$

The engineers require a material with a Brinell Hardness Number (BHN) between 3900 MPa and 4100 MPa for the pushrod.

Determine, by calculation, whether the material being tested is suitable for the pushrod. State Yes or No and show your working.

Refer to information on page 6 of the Resource Booklet. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
BHN Formula & Calculation (3 marks):
1. Formula from Resource Booklet:
$$\text{BHN} = 102 \times \frac{2F}{\pi D\left(D - \sqrt{D^2 - D_i^2}\right)}$$
2. Substitute values ($F = 10\text{ kN}$, $D = 10\text{ mm}$, $D_i = 0.60\text{ mm}$):
$$\sqrt{D^2 - D_i^2} = \sqrt{10^2 - 0.60^2} = \sqrt{100 - 0.36} = \sqrt{99.64} \approx 9.98198\text{ mm}$$
$$D - \sqrt{D^2 - D_i^2} = 10 - 9.98198 = 0.018016\text{ mm}$$
$$\text{Denominator} = \pi \times 10 \times 0.018016 = 0.565997$$
$$\text{BHN} = 102 \times \frac{20}{0.565997} = 102 \times 35.3359 = \mathbf{3604\text{ MPa}} \quad (\text{allow } 3600\text{ to } 3605\text{ MPa}) \quad [2\text{ marks}]$$
3. Suitability judgment: Since $3604\text{ MPa}$ does not lie within the required range of $3900 - 4100\text{ MPa}$, the material is not suitable. Answer: No [1 mark]

questions.question: 4(b)(i)
questions.summary: Calculate the diameter in mm of the polymer rope given cross-sectional area of 2.84 x 10^-4 m^2.
questions.prompt:
During use at sea, The Snake described on pages 4 and 5 of the Resource Booklet is tethered to a fixed buoy by a rope as shown in Fig. 3. The design engineers responsible for The Snake want to calculate the diameter of the polymer rope.

Data for the rope under investigation is given in Fig. 6 on page 7 of the Resource Booklet ($A = 2.84 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$).

Calculate the diameter in mm of the polymer rope. Give your answer to 1 decimal place and show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Diameter Calculation (3 marks):
1. Area of circular cross-section: $A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4} \implies d = \sqrt{\frac{4A}{\pi}}$ [1 mark]
2. Substitute area $A = 2.84 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$:
$$d = \sqrt{\frac{4 \times 2.84 \times 10^{-4}}{\pi}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.001136}{\pi}} = \sqrt{0.0003616} \approx 0.019016\text{ m} \quad [1\text{ mark}]$$
3. Convert to millimetres: $d = 0.019016 \times 1000 = \mathbf{19.0\text{ mm}}$ (to 1 d.p.) [1 mark]

questions.question: 4(b)(ii)
questions.summary: Calculate tensile stress in N/m^2 in the polymer rope under a tensile force of 4200 N.
questions.prompt:
Tests have been carried out to determine that the average tensile force in the polymer rope will be 4200 N.

Calculate the tensile stress (in N/m²) in the polymer rope when the tensile force is 4200 N. Give your answer in N/m² and show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Tensile Stress Calculation (3 marks):
1. Recall formula: $\sigma = \frac{F}{A}$ [1 mark]
2. Substitute values ($F = 4200\text{ N}$, $A = 2.84 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m}^2$):
$$\sigma = \frac{4200}{2.84 \times 10^{-4}} = \frac{4200}{0.000284} \quad [1\text{ mark}]$$
3. Calculate stress: $\sigma = \mathbf{14\,788\,732\text{ N/m}^2}$ (allow $1.48 \times 10^7\text{ N/m}^2$ or $14.79\text{ MPa}$) [1 mark]

questions.question: 4(b)(iii)
questions.summary: Calculate the extension of the 20 m polymer rope in metres using Young's modulus E = 1.3 x 10^9 N/m^2.
questions.prompt:
When the polymer rope is under tension it will stretch.

Calculate the extension of the polymer rope in m when the stress is at the value you calculated in part (b)(ii) ($\sigma = 14\,788\,732\text{ N/m}^2$, $L_0 = 20\text{ m}$, $E = 1.3 \times 10^9\text{ N/m}^2$).

Give your answer to 3 decimal places and show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Young's Modulus & Extension Steps (3 marks):
1. Recall relationships: $E = \frac{\text{Stress}}{\text{Strain}} \implies \epsilon = \frac{\sigma}{E}$ [1 mark]
2. Calculate strain $\epsilon$:
$$\epsilon = \frac{14\,788\,732}{1.3 \times 10^9} \approx 0.0113759 \quad [1\text{ mark}]$$
3. Calculate extension $\Delta L = \epsilon \times L_0$ ($L_0 = 20\text{ m}$):
$$\Delta L = 0.0113759 \times 20 = 0.2275\text{ m} \approx \mathbf{0.228\text{ m}} \quad (\text{to 3 d.p.}) \quad [1\text{ mark}]$$

questions.summary: Critically evaluate any three factors influencing the commercial viability of The Snake WEC prototype.
questions.prompt:
The Snake WEC described on pages 4 and 5 of the Resource Booklet is a prototype product in the development stage.

The stakeholders of The Snake are concerned about its commercial viability and have asked for an evaluation of a range of factors:
• how well the product performs
• technical difficulty of manufacture and materials selection
• cost and profits
• maintenance requirements
• size and appearance.

Choose any three factors from the list above. Critically evaluate the ways in which they influence the commercial viability of The Snake.

Use information on pages 4, 5 and 7 of the Resource Booklet. [*14]
questions.markscheme_text:
Level 4 (11–14 marks): Comprehensive critical evaluation of 3 chosen factors with direct, detailed references to The Snake WEC, offshore deployment realities, and commercial financial viability.
Level 3 (7–10 marks): Good critical evaluation of 3 factors with clear application.
Level 2 (4–6 marks): Adequate evaluation of factors with general points.
Level 1 (1–3 marks): Limited descriptive response.

Indicative Content for Factors:
• How well the product performs: Electrical power generation output (kWh) depends on ocean wave frequency and wave amplitude; irregular wave cycles cause fluctuating generation requiring complex onboard power conditioning; prototype efficiency vs theoretical maximum.
• Technical difficulty of manufacture & materials selection: Marine-grade materials essential (corrosion-resistant stainless steel 316, marine bronze, UV-stabilised composite polymers, antifouling coatings); dynamic waterproof seals around reciprocating pushrods must withstand high hydrostatic pressure without leaking; large fabrication tolerances.
• Costs and profits: High capital expenditure (CapEx) for tooling, fabrication, and specialised offshore towing vessels; long return on investment (payback period) reliant on government renewable feed-in tariffs; competitive levelized cost of energy (LCOE) compared to offshore wind and solar.
• Maintenance requirements: Offshore maintenance is notoriously hazardous and weather-dependent; salt encrustation, bio-fouling (barnacles/seaweed), and tether rope fatigue wear; remote wireless telemetry helps condition monitoring to avoid catastrophic offshore failure.
• Size and appearance: Low visual profile on the horizon reduces coastal NIMBY objections compared to towering wind turbines; modular scalable length allows flexible expansion based on client budget.

questions.question: 1(a)(i)

questions.question: 1(c)(i)
questions.summary: Calculate output terminal voltage of the battery pack with 3 parallel rows of 10 series cells at 3.6 V each.
questions.prompt:
One model of electric scooter has a rechargeable battery pack which is made from 30 individual ‘18650’ lithium-ion cells. The 18650 cell is a standardised component. Fig. 1.3 shows how the cells are connected to form the complete battery pack.

Each cell produces a voltage of 3.6 V.

Calculate the output terminal voltage from the battery pack in volts to 0 decimal places. Show your working. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Calculation (2 marks):
1. Identify series configuration: Each branch has 10 cells in series [1 mark]
2. Calculate terminal voltage: $V = 10 \times 3.6\text{ V} = \mathbf{36\text{ V}}$ [1 mark]
(Note: Parallel connection of identical branches does not increase voltage; 108 V earns 0 marks)

questions.question: 1(c)(ii)
questions.summary: Explain one advantage of building the battery pack with three parallel groups of cells.
questions.prompt: Explain one advantage of building the battery pack with three parallel groups of cells. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Up to 2 marks for explained advantage:
• Tripled capacity (Ah) and range: Connecting 3 branches in parallel multiplies total charge capacity by 3 (1), directly extending the scooter's operational riding range between charges (1).
• Lower internal resistance & higher discharge current: Three parallel paths divide internal resistance by 3 ($R_p = R/3$) (1), enabling the pack to deliver higher peak current without excessive thermal heating or voltage sag (1).
• Fault tolerance / redundancy: If one branch suffers a cell degradation, the remaining two branches can still deliver 36 V to limp home safely (1).

questions.question: 1(c)(iii)
questions.summary: State one benefit to a manufacturer of using standard 18650 cells rather than designing a bespoke battery pack.
questions.prompt: State one benefit to a scooter manufacturer of using standard 18650 cells in a battery pack rather than designing a bespoke battery pack. Justify your answer. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
• Economy of scale & lower cost: Standard 18650 cells are mass-produced in massive global volumes by Tier-1 suppliers (1), resulting in drastically cheaper unit costs than designing custom cell form factors (1).
• Supply chain security & second sourcing: Standardised cell dimensions allow the manufacturer to source from multiple certified vendors (1), avoiding single-supplier production delays or factory bottlenecks (1).
• Proven safety certifications: Standard cells have extensive pre-existing UN 38.3, UL, and CE transport/safety testing (1), eliminating the heavy time and financial burden of certifying custom cells (1).

questions.question: 1(d)(i)
questions.summary: Show by calculation that the kinetic energy gain in the first second is 175 J for a 250 W motor at 70% efficiency.
questions.prompt:
The motor in an electric scooter is rated at 250 W. The efficiency of the motor is 70%.

The rider accelerates the electric scooter at full power from a standstill on level ground.

Determine by calculation that the gain in kinetic energy of the electric scooter and rider in the first second is 175 J. You must ignore the effects of friction and air resistance. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Calculation (2 marks):
1. Electrical energy consumed in $1\text{ s}$: $E_{\text{in}} = P \times t = 250\text{ W} \times 1\text{ s} = 250\text{ J}$ [1 mark]
2. Mechanical energy output (KE gain): $\text{KE} = 250\text{ J} \times 0.70 = \mathbf{175\text{ J}}$ [1 mark]

questions.question: 1(d)(ii)
questions.summary: Calculate the speed in m/s (1 d.p.) of the 85 kg scooter and rider given 175 J KE in 1 second.
questions.prompt:
The total mass of the electric scooter and rider is 85 kg. The electric scooter reaches a constant speed after 3 seconds.

Use the information in part (d)(i) to calculate the constant speed of the electric scooter when it reaches 3 seconds. Give your answer in m/s to 1 decimal place and show your working.

You must assume that the power output from the motor remains constant. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Kinetic Energy to Speed Steps (3 marks):
1. Total KE or single-second formula: $\text{KE} = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 \implies v = \sqrt{\frac{2\text{KE}}{m}}$ [1 mark]
2. Substitute values: $v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 175}{85}} = \sqrt{\frac{350}{85}} = \sqrt{4.1176} \approx 2.029\text{ m/s}$ (or with $3\text{ s}$ total energy $525\text{ J}$: $v = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 525}{85}} = \sqrt{12.35} \approx 3.5\text{ m/s}$) [1 mark]
3. Correct rounding: $\mathbf{2.0\text{ m/s}}$ (or $3.5\text{ m/s}$) [1 mark]

questions.question: 2(a)(i)
questions.summary: Calculate total cross-sectional area of copper in the wire made of 50 strands of 0.25 mm diameter.
questions.prompt:
Fig. 2.1 shows the structure of a stranded electrical wire.

The stranded electrical wire in Fig. 2.1 is made from 50 strands of copper. The diameter of each strand is 0.25 mm.

Calculate the total cross-sectional area of copper in the wire. Give your answer in mm² to 2 decimal places and show your working. [3]
questions.markscheme_text:
Area Calculation (3 marks):
1. Area formula: $A = \pi r^2 = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}$ [1 mark]
2. Area of one strand ($d = 0.25\text{ mm}$, $r = 0.125\text{ mm}$):
$$A_1 = \pi \times (0.125)^2 \approx 0.049087\text{ mm}^2 \quad [1\text{ mark}]$$
3. Total area of 50 strands:
$$A_{\text{total}} = 50 \times 0.049087 = 2.45437\text{ mm}^2 \approx \mathbf{2.45\text{ mm}^2} \quad [1\text{ mark}]$$

questions.question: 2(a)(ii)
questions.summary: Calculate percentage error between calculated area 2.45 mm^2 and expected area 2.50 mm^2.
questions.prompt:
The manufacturer states that the cross-sectional area of copper in the wire is 2.50 mm².

Calculate the percentage error between the cross-sectional area calculated in part (a)(i) and the expected area of 2.50 mm². Show your working. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Percentage Error (2 marks):
1. Formula: $\%\text{ error} = \frac{|\text{Expected} - \text{Actual}|}{\text{Expected}} \times 100$ [1 mark]
2. Calculation:
$$\%\text{ error} = \frac{2.50 - 2.45}{2.50} \times 100 = \frac{0.05}{2.50} \times 100 = 0.02 \times 100 = \mathbf{2\%} \quad [1\text{ mark}]$$

questions.question: 2(a)(iii)
questions.summary: Calculate resistance in ohms of 3 m length of stranded copper wire using resistivity 1.72 x 10^-8 ohm-m and area 2.50 mm^2.
questions.prompt:
The resistance of a wire can be calculated using the formula:
$$R = \frac{\rho L}{A}$$
where $R$ is resistance (Ω), $\rho$ is resistivity ($1.72 \times 10^{-8}\,\Omega\text{m}$), $L$ is length ($3\text{ m}$), $A$ is cross-sectional area ($2.50\text{ mm}^2$).

Using the value 2.50 mm² for the cross-sectional area, calculate the resistance in Ω of a 3 m length of the electrical stranded wire shown in Fig. 2.1.

You must not round off your answer. Show your working. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Resistivity Calculation (2 marks):
1. Convert area to $\text{m}^2$: $A = 2.50\text{ mm}^2 = 2.50 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^2$ [1 mark]
2. Calculate $R$:
$$R = \frac{1.72 \times 10^{-8} \times 3}{2.50 \times 10^{-6}} = \frac{5.16 \times 10^{-8}}{2.50 \times 10^{-6}} = \mathbf{0.02064\,\Omega} \quad [1\text{ mark}]$$

questions.question: 2(a)(iv)
questions.summary: Calculate voltage drop along the 3 m wire when it carries 25 A.
questions.prompt: Use your answer from part (a)(iii) to calculate the voltage drop along the 3 m length of wire when it carries 25 A. Show your working. [2]
questions.markscheme_text:
Ohm's Law Calculation (2 marks):
1. Formula: $V = I \times R$ [1 mark]

questions.summary: Critically examine factors a company developing a new stand-up paddle board needs to consider, referencing different stakeholders.
questions.prompt:

Clear, developed narrative covering design, economic, safety, and manufacturing considerations.

questions.question: 3(a)
questions.summary: Determine by calculation the most suitable stand-up paddle board from Fig. 7 for an 80 kg user carrying 15 kg gear in sea water.
questions.prompt:
Stand-up paddle boards are made in different sizes to suit the weight of the user and the load they wish to carry. The Resource Booklet contains data for five stand-up paddle boards.

A user has a mass of 80 kg and they will also carry a backpack of mass 12 kg and a paddle of mass 3 kg. They will use the stand-up paddle board in the sea.

Determine by calculation the most suitable stand-up paddle board for this user, ignoring the weight of the paddle board.

Archimedes Principle Sizing Steps (6 marks):
1. Total load mass: $M = 80\text{ kg} + 12\text{ kg} + 3\text{ kg} = \mathbf{95\text{ kg}}$ [1 mark]
2. Total weight force: $W = M \times g = 95 \times 9.81 = \mathbf{931.95\text{ N}}$ [1 mark]
3. Rearrange buoyant force equation: $B = \rho V g \implies V = \frac{B}{\rho g}$ [1 mark]
4. Calculate displaced water volume (sea water $\rho = 1025\text{ kg/m}^3$):
$$V = \frac{931.95}{1025 \times 9.81} = \frac{931.95}{10055.25} \approx 0.09268\text{ m}^3 \quad [1\text{ mark}]$$
5. Convert to litres and apply half-submerged rule:
$$V_{\text{displaced}} = 0.09268 \times 1000 = 92.68\text{ litres (or 93 L)}$$
$$\text{Total board volume required} = 2 \times 92.68 = \mathbf{185.36\text{ litres (or 186 L)}} \quad [1\text{ mark}]$$
6. Select matching board from Fig. 7:
Board-14 has a volume of $185\text{ litres}$ (closest match to 185.4 L). Answer: Board-14 [1 mark]

questions.summary: Determine technical solutions for the PB Speedometer: removable sensor mounting & detection, and GENIE-14 circuit & 5-LED bar graph flowchart.
questions.prompt:
A start-up company wishes to develop an electronic Paddle Board (PB) Speedometer which gives an indication to the user of the speed that the stand-up paddle board is travelling through the water. Information for the proposed product is given on page 8 of the Resource Booklet.

The design engineers have been instructed to solve the following two issues to help with the development of the PB Speedometer.
Issue 1: To measure the speed that the stand-up paddle board travels through the water, a suitable sensor needs to be designed. This sensor must be able to be firmly attached to an inflated stand-up paddle board but must be removable when the stand-up paddle board is deflated and packed away. The electronic output signal from the sensor will be processed by a microcontroller.
Issue 2: The signal from the sensor will be processed by a GENIE-14 microcontroller and the speed of the stand-up paddle board will be displayed to the user on a 5-LED bar graph display. Details of the GENIE-14 microcontroller and the bar graph display are shown on page 8 of the Resource Booklet. A circuit diagram and a program flowchart are required to enable the PB Speedometer system to function as described. The circuit diagram must show how the sensor and the five LEDs are connected to the microcontroller. The program flowchart should indicate how increasing speed causes more LEDs to light.

Use sketches and/or notes to determine suitable technical solutions that overcome the two issues identified. Refer to information on page 8 of the Resource Booklet. [16]
questions.markscheme_text:
Award up to 8 marks for Issue 1 and up to 8 marks for Issue 2 (Total 16 marks):

Issue 1 Breakdown (8 marks):
• Sensor Design & Operation (4 marks): Identifies valid mechanism: miniature water impeller driving a tiny DC generator to produce variable DC voltage (Method 1), or magnetic paddle wheel triggering a reed switch/Hall effect sensor to produce speed-proportional frequency pulses (Method 2); water flow path and waterproof casing detailed.
• Attachment / Detachment Mechanism (4 marks): Shows non-destructive mounting system: heavy-duty clamp around board rail, fin-box slide-and-click locking tab, or heavy-duty velcro/suction strap; securely holds sensor during paddling and easily releases when deflating without puncturing PVC.

Issue 2 Breakdown (8 marks):
• Circuit Diagram (4 marks): Power supply (+5V, 0V) connected to GENIE-14; sensor output routed to input pin (e.g. Analogue A0 for voltage, or Digital D1 for pulse counting); 5 outputs (Q0–Q4) connected to 5 LEDs of bar graph with correct forward polarity and individual protective current-limiting resistors (e.g. $330\,\Omega$).
• Program Flowchart (4 marks): Start block; reads sensor input; sequential comparison against rising threshold variables (`sensor > 10`, `sensor > 20`, `sensor > 30`, `sensor > 40`, `sensor > 50`); activates corresponding incremental LED outputs (`LED 1 on`, `LED 1,2 on`, etc.); turns off upper LEDs as speed drops; infinite loop.

questions.question: When variable resistor VR1 is set at 20 \(\Omega\), the fan runs at half maximum speed with a current of 250 mA. Calculate the power dissipated in variable resistor VR1 when set at 20 \(\Omega\). Give your answer in W and show your working.

questions.question: Use the information in Fig. 5 of the Resource Booklet to calculate the total internal volume of the funnel (both sections). Give your answer in cm3 to 2 decimal places. Show your working. Volume of a cone = 1/3 pi r^2 h.
questions.markscheme_text:
**Six marks total:**

1. Identify conical dimensions and radii:  
   $$R_1 = \frac{110\text{ mm}}{2} = 55\text{ mm} = 5.5\text{ cm} \quad [1]$$
   $$R_2 = \frac{20\text{ mm}}{2} = 10\text{ mm} = 1.0\text{ cm}$$
   $$\text{Height of conical section } h = 49\text{ mm} = 4.9\text{ cm}$$

2. Calculate full apex height \(H\) of cone by similar triangles:  
   $$\frac{H}{55} = \frac{H - 49}{10} \implies 10H = 55H - 2695 \implies 45H = 2695 \implies H = 59.889\text{ mm} = 5.989\text{ cm} \quad [1]$$

3. Calculate volume of large cone:  
   $$V_{\text{large}} = \frac{1}{3}\pi R_1^2 H = \frac{1}{3}\pi (5.5)^2 (5.989) = 189.72\text{ cm}^3 \quad [1]$$

4. Calculate volume of small cut-off cone:  
   $$h_2 = 59.889 - 49 = 10.889\text{ mm} = 1.089\text{ cm}$$
   $$V_{\text{small}} = \frac{1}{3}\pi R_2^2 h_2 = \frac{1}{3}\pi (1.0)^2 (1.089) = 1.14\text{ cm}^3 \quad [1]$$

5. Volume of conical frustum:  
   $$V_{\text{frustum}} = 189.72 - 1.14 = 188.58\text{ cm}^3 \quad (\text{or via frustum formula: } 188.92\text{ cm}^3) \quad [1]$$

6. Add cylindrical volume and give total:  
   $$V_{\text{total}} = 188.92 + 4.7 = \mathbf{193.6\text{ cm}^3} \quad (\text{accept } 193.28\text{ cm}^3 - 193.62\text{ cm}^3) \quad [1]$$

questions.question: WW wants to explore the feasibility of adding a wind speed sensor to the PWS. The design engineers have to solve the following two issues: Issue 1: The sensor must produce output electrical signals which could be processed by a PICAXE 14M2 microcontroller. Use sketches and/or notes to further develop the wind speed sensor shown in Fig. 9 of the Resource Booklet. Issue 2: Draw a circuit diagram to show how the wind sensor electronic components and the radio transmitter components connect to the PICAXE 14M2, and draw a program flowchart that indicates how rotation speed is monitored and data transmitted. Refer to pages 7–9 of the Resource Booklet.
questions.markscheme_text:
**16 marks total (8 marks for Issue 1 + 8 marks for Issue 2):**

**Issue 1: Mechanical & Sensor Development (8 marks):**
- **Rotation & Bearing Support:** Low-friction stainless steel / ceramic ball bearings housed inside the fixed base to allow free rotation of the vertical rod with minimal wind resistance.
- **Sensing Component Selection:**
  - *Option A:* Slotted optical switch (phototransistor + IR LED) with a slotted encoder disc mounted on the rotating rod.
  - *Option B:* Hall effect magnetic sensor or reed switch actuated by a small neodymium magnet embedded in the rotating hub.
- **Signal Description:** Digital pulses whose frequency is directly proportional to rotational velocity (wind speed).

**Issue 2: Circuit Diagram & Program Flowchart (8 marks):**
- **Circuit Diagram:**
  - PICAXE 14M2 powered from +V (Pin 1) and 0V (Pin 14).
  - Sensor output connected to digital input pin (e.g. C.3) with appropriate pull-up/pull-down resistor.
  - Serial Data Out (pin B.0 / Sout) connected to NKM2401 Serial Data In (pin 2).
  - NKM2401 module interfaced with A434 radio transmitter, including 10 kΩ pull-down resistor and 100 nF decoupling capacitors across supply rails.
- **Program Flowchart:**
  - Start $\to$ Initialize pulse counter variable $= 0$.
  - Start a fixed timer loop (e.g. 1.0 second or use hardware `count` command).
  - Increment pulse counter on each rising edge from sensor input.
  - When timer elapses, compute wind speed: $\text{speed} = \text{pulses} \times \text{calibration factor}$.
  - Transmit data string via `serout` command to radio transmitter.
  - Reset counter and repeat monitoring loop.
